agencies.lines: Milwaukee County Transit System: CONNECT 1 bus rapid transit (rapid) and the bus routes that run every 15 minutes at the morning peak
Madison Metro: Rapid Route A (rapid transit), plus Routes B, C, D and 80, which like Route A run at least every 15 minutes on weekdays
Eau Claire Transit: Routes 9 and 19 run every 20 minutes, so they count only in the wider definitions

district.text: Every Wisconsin city with rail or rapid transit stops must zone a district where apartment buildings are allowed by right, at least 15 homes per acre, covering 15% of the land within ¼ mile of rail and rapid stops. The city picks the land. The model treats the district as spread at random over that land.

median_line.note: A median line of real cases is shown only when there are at least 4 comparable cases. Here the central line is already the average of the 11 district places, so no separate median line is shown.

range90.coverage: The unwidened range held the true average in 84.5% of test runs, below 90%, so it was widened. A check on fake effects held only 69%, so the range may still be narrow.
range90.method: Place bootstrap of the 11 district places (2,000 draws), widened ×1.1827 about 10,028 after a coverage test: the unwidened range was 4,866 to 15,361.
range90.unit: extra homes permitted near major transit stops, Wisconsin, 2027–2031
range90.years_method: Each end of the range is spread over the years by the same yearly shares as the lines, so each year's ends add up to the five-year ends.

scenarios.evidence: edge test at district boundaries, 5 places
scenarios.info: Just inside a district's boundary versus just outside it, before and after the rezoning, in the 5 places whose two sides were alike beforehand: about 88 extra new homes per 100 acres of district lots a year. Applied to a district of 15% of Wisconsin's land within ¼ mile of rail and rapid stops, for five years: about 3,960 extra homes over 2027–2031 (90% range about 2,280 to 5,790). It counts only the rezoned lots' own gain, not any lift to nearby lots, so it is a floor. Fake boundaries drawn where nothing changed show about zero. The former lower line (the best lot model, 824) is on How sure.
scenarios.label: Lower: the rezoned parcels' own gain only
scenarios.range_note: 90% range from resampling stretches of district boundary
scenarios.source: Edge test (T3) direct-effect floor, 5 balance-passing places: 3,958.0 extra homes over 2027-2031 (90% 2,279.5 to 5,791.0), reference/tod_causal_lines.csv; 11-place build-up

scenarios.info: The 11 places' districts covered on average about 12% of the land within ¼ mile (from 2% to 26%), a little less than the law's 15%; this line keeps their effect as measured, without scaling it to 15%. Their average measured effect within ¼ mile of their reform stops, compared with similar stops without reform, before and after: about 34 extra new homes per 100 acres of lots a year. Applied to Wisconsin's lots within ¼ mile of rail and rapid stops (about 4,870 acres in Milwaukee and Madison, scaled to the state by its share of that land, ×1.227) for five years: about 10,030 extra homes over 2027–2031 (range about 7,580 to 12,010, leaving out one place at a time). No model we tried beat this average on places it had not seen, so by the rule set before the results it is the central line. Caution: those cities chose their district land themselves, often land builders already wanted; a state mandate may do less. Land beyond ¼ mile counts zero. The earlier central line for the broader law (the average reform city at 71% coverage) is shown on How sure as a comparison.
scenarios.label: Central: the average district place, across about 12% of lots within ¼ mile of transit
scenarios.range_note: leaving out one place at a time
scenarios.source: Average of the 11 district places' measured effect within 1/4 mile: 10,028.1 extra homes over 2027-2031 (range 7,579.8 to 12,010.4), reference/tod_optiond_line.csv; 11-place build-up

scenarios.evidence: measured near 11 US places' stops, scaled to the law's 15%
scenarios.info: Same 11 places as the central line. Their districts covered about 12% of the land within ¼ mile; the law asks for 15%. This line scales their effect up to 15%, in step with how much land each place zoned. That is about 42 extra new homes per 100 lot acres a year. Applied to Wisconsin's lots within ¼ mile of rail and rapid stops, for five years: about 12,520 extra homes over 2027–2031 (range about 9,090 to 16,770, leaving out one place at a time). Caution: among the 11 places, bigger districts gained less per acre, so scaling up leans on the smallest districts. Two other readings are what-ifs on How sure: rezoned stops on new transit lines (13,451), and the same minus growth already under way before the reforms (5,624).
scenarios.label: Upper: the average district place, scaled up to 15% of lots within ¼ mile of transit
scenarios.range_note: leaving out one place at a time
scenarios.source: Average district place scaled to a 15% district by the pooled ratio: 12,520.8 extra homes over 2027-2031 (leave one place out 9,089.2 to 16,771.1), reference/tod_causal_lines.csv (from reference/tod_optiond_line.csv); 11-place build-up

side_lines.label: Average district place, 11 places (the former central)
side_lines.note: The average measured effect of the 11 places that zoned a district near their stops, applied to Wisconsin's land within ¼ mile.

side_lines.label: Edge test, rezoned lots' own gain (5 places)
side_lines.note: Only the gain on the rezoned lots themselves, just inside against just outside district boundaries.

side_lines.label: Average scaled to a 15% district (11 places)
side_lines.note: The same average, scaled up from the places' 12% of land to the law's 15%; bigger districts gained less per acre.

side_lines.label: Rezoning near new transit lines, 2×2 (9 places)
side_lines.note: Rezoned stops on lines that were new at the time, against new-line stops that were not rezoned.

side_lines.label: Same minus the growth already under way before the reforms
side_lines.note: The 2×2 reading after taking out the faster growth those stops already had before any reform (its before-reform check failed).

timing_caveat: The places' effects were measured over the years after each reform. The model places that effect inside 2027–2031, the law's first five years. Much of a real law's effect may come after 2031, so the yearly path is the least certain part of these numbers.
